PHẦN A: 1. Many analysts believe that some form of economic disruption is inevitable as automation spreads across traditional industries. — "Inevitable" nghĩa là "không thể tránh khỏi"; thường đi với "seem/become inevitable", khác với "unpredictable" (không thể đoán trước). 2. City planners warn that a housing shortage looks imminent unless new construction is authorised within the next few years. — "Imminent" chỉ điều "sắp xảy ra, cận kề"; hay đi với "imminent danger/collapse/breakthrough". 3. Changing demography, particularly an ageing population, is likely to place growing strain on healthcare and pension systems. — "Demography" là ngành nghiên cứu dân số; phân biệt với "demographics" (số liệu dân số cụ thể). 4. Government projections suggest that renewable energy could supply most of the national grid within a few decades. — "Projections" (số nhiều) chỉ các dự báo dựa trên xu hướng hiện tại, thường đi với "economic/population projections". 5. Urban planners often model a worst-case scenario to make sure new infrastructure can cope with future population growth. — "Scenario" là kịch bản/tình huống giả định; collocation phổ biến "a worst-case scenario", "a plausible scenario". 6. The pace of change in artificial intelligence over the past few years has been genuinely unprecedented. — "Unprecedented" nghĩa là "chưa từng có tiền lệ"; hay đi với "unprecedented levels/scale/growth". 7. It would be unwise to speculate too confidently about exactly which jobs will disappear, since technology evolves unpredictably. — "Speculate" là suy đoán không có bằng chứng chắc chắn; giới từ đi kèm là "about/on", không dùng "for". 8. Many economists argue that disruptive technologies such as automation and AI will fundamentally reorganise the labour market. — "Disruptive" trong ngữ cảnh công nghệ/kinh doanh mang nghĩa tích cực (đột phá), không phải nghĩa tiêu cực thông thường. 9. Strategic foresight allows governments to prepare for demographic and environmental pressures long before a crisis erupts. — "Foresight" là danh từ không đếm được, chỉ khả năng nhìn xa trông rộng; trái nghĩa với "hindsight". 10. Some novelists imagine a dystopian future in which surveillance technology has eroded nearly all personal privacy. — "Dystopian" mô tả một xã hội tương lai đen tối, áp bức; trái nghĩa với "utopian". 11. The shift towards remote working during recent years represents a genuine paradigm shift in how organisations think about productivity. — "Paradigm shift" là sự thay đổi căn bản trong tư duy/cách tiếp cận; chữ "g" trong "paradigm" câm khi phát âm. 12. If current trends continue, the trajectory of global urbanisation points towards ever larger and more crowded megacities. — "Trajectory" chỉ hướng phát triển của một xu hướng; ở đây dùng nghĩa ẩn dụ, không phải nghĩa vật lý.

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: It is likely that remote working will become increasingly common in the years ahead. Band 8: Remote working looks set to become the norm rather than the exception, as organisations increasingly embrace flexible arrangements. 2. Band 7: Many experts predict that automation will eliminate certain types of jobs. Band 8: Many experts argue that disruptive automation will render a range of routine occupations largely obsolete, even if entirely new roles emerge in their place. 3. Band 7: Nobody can predict with certainty what society will look like in fifty years' time. Band 8: Given how inherently speculative long-range forecasting is, it seems unwise to claim any certainty about society half a century from now. 4. Band 7: Governments should show foresight and plan for problems before a crisis develops. Band 8: Were governments to cultivate greater strategic foresight, many looming crises might be pre-empted rather than merely managed after the fact. 5. Band 7: New inventions often bring about unexpected changes in the way people live. Band 8: It is often disruptive innovation, rather than incremental progress, that triggers a genuine paradigm shift in everyday life. 6. Band 7: Some predictions turn out to be inaccurate because circumstances change so rapidly. Band 8: Not only do circumstances shift unpredictably, but forecasts that once seemed plausible may well prove wide of the mark within a matter of years. 7. Band 7: It is probable that cities will expand considerably over the coming decades. Band 8: Should current demographic trends persist, our cities' trajectory points towards unprecedented levels of urban density within a generation. 8. Band 7: It is difficult to know for certain whether a new technology will transform society. Band 8: Whether a given technology will prove genuinely transformative or merely a passing trend is something only time will tell.

passages.text: The phrase "smart city" entered the international vocabulary of urban policy around 2008, propelled by a marketing campaign from a single multinational technology firm. By 2015 the term had been adopted, with varying conviction, by municipalities from Songdo to Toronto, and was used to describe an extraordinarily wide assortment of measures: real-time bus tracking, sensor-equipped streetlights, predictive policing systems, garbage bins that report their fill level, and entire purpose-built districts assembled around a layer of digital infrastructure. The breadth of the category, in the view of the geographer Shannon Mattern, has always been part of the difficulty. When a term can refer to almost anything, it commits to almost nothing, and the resulting evangelism can pass for analysis.

A more pointed critique has come from the technology writer Adam Greenfield. In his 2017 book Radical Technologies and the related essays that followed, Greenfield argued that the smart-city concept rests on a category mistake. Cities, he contends, are not problems amenable to optimisation; they are arenas of contested life, in which the very identification of what counts as a problem is already a political act. To install sensors on every kerb and to feed the resulting data into a unified control room, on this reading, does not so much resolve urban tensions as displace them into a domain that residents are poorly positioned to scrutinise. The municipal dashboard appears neutral, but its categories were chosen by someone, somewhere, for purposes that are seldom disclosed.

An adjacent line of work has been developed by Kate Crawford, an Australian-American researcher now based at the University of Southern California. Crawford has argued, in her 2021 book Atlas of AI, that the apparently weightless layer of algorithmic infrastructure rests on a substantial material substrate: rare-earth mining in Inner Mongolia, lithium extraction in the Atacama, the energy footprint of large model training, and the labour of low-paid workers who annotate the data on which urban algorithms depend. The smart city, in Crawford's analysis, is the visible terminus of a long and largely invisible global supply chain. To treat it as a self-contained technological achievement is, she suggests, to engage in a particularly modern form of geographical forgetting.

Defenders of the model would respond that these critiques apply unevenly. Anthony Townsend, an urbanist who has written sympathetically about smart-city pilots, has noted that the same technological tools can be deployed within radically different governance frameworks. A Barcelona-style "superblock" programme, in which sensor data are used primarily to monitor air quality and adjust public-space allocation, is structurally different from a Songdo-style command centre in which surveillance and operational efficiency are paramount. Townsend has called for a distinction between civic-led applications, which extend the capacity of public agencies to deliver services, and vendor-led deployments, in which procurement contracts effectively delegate strategic decisions to suppliers. The critiques developed by Greenfield and Crawford, he argues, land squarely on the second category and only partially on the first.

A particularly instructive case is the abortive Sidewalk Labs project, which proposed in 2017 to develop a twelve-acre waterfront site in Toronto into a fully sensorised district. The plan attracted intense scrutiny over data governance, intellectual property and the terms on which residents would, in effect, consent to continuous monitoring. By 2020, after a wave of resignations from advisory boards and sustained criticism from the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the project had been withdrawn. The withdrawal was variously interpreted: by Sidewalk Labs as a casualty of the pandemic, by its critics as evidence that vendor-led urbanism could not survive serious democratic scrutiny. Both readings contain some truth, although the second appears, with hindsight, to carry more weight.

What emerges from the wider literature is a more sober appraisal of what technological infrastructure can and cannot do for cities. Targeted applications, calibrated to a specific service and accountable to a specific public agency, have produced measurable benefits: a 2022 review by the Brookings Institution counted modest but reliable gains in air-quality monitoring, water-leak detection and traffic-signal optimisation across dozens of mid-sized European and North American cities. Sweeping reorganisations, by contrast, have a poorer track record. Songdo, despite a decade of investment, has struggled to attract the population for which it was designed; the prospective Saudi project NEOM has yet to demonstrate its more ambitious claims; and the term "smart" itself has largely fallen out of favour in the policy papers of the OECD and the World Bank.

None of this implies that digital tools have no role in urban governance. The contrary case is plain enough: traffic engineering, public-health surveillance and water systems all depend on data that did not exist a generation ago. What appears to have shifted is the rhetorical envelope around those tools. The earlier promise of comprehensive optimisation has given way, in many quarters, to a more limited claim about specific instruments addressing specific problems, with explicit attention to who controls the data and on whose terms.

Whether this more chastened version of the smart city will survive the next decade remains uncertain. The financial pressure on technology firms to redeploy the same platforms into ever-larger commitments has not vanished, and the appeal of a single dashboard for a complex city remains seductive. Yet the experience of the past fifteen years has begun to install a useful intellectual habit: the demand that any urban-technology proposal be accompanied by the question of who benefits, who is monitored, and who decides. That habit, if it persists, may prove to be the most durable legacy of the smart-city decade.

audio_scripts.text: Hi everyone — awesome to see such a packed room. Today's lecture extends our urban-futures series, and I wanna focus on the empirical literature concerning smart-city horizons and how vertical-farming infrastructure is being folded into municipal planning. [pause:5s] The conceptual framework I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Anand Vyshakh — that's V-Y-S-H-A-K-H, with a Y after the V and an H at the end, no hyphen. Vyshakh's 2020 monograph reframed smart-city scenarios from a technology checklist into what he calls "convergence horizon theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal forecast cohort I'll reference today was first canvassed in 2020 — sorry, let me correct that, 2019; the published descriptive statistics in 2020 covered data collected in 2019. So whenever I refer to the baseline forecast year, please record 2019. [pause:3s] Right, you guys, a quick tense-orientation note. Vyshakh's framework USED TO be operationalised with single-domain Delphi panels — energy alone, or transport alone — NOW the field deploys cross-domain integrated scenario panels combining food, energy, transport, and waste, and from 2030 a global consortium WILL be incorporating real-time digital-twin telemetry into the same forecasting pipeline. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, cross-domain integrated panels. [pause:3s] Okay, moving to terminology. The neighbourhood-scale food-production concept Vyshakh foregrounds — a closed-loop building-integrated growing system that recycles its own water and nutrients without external soil input — is termed an "autotrophic block". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: vertical farm, urban greenhouse, indoor garden. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Vyshakh's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is autotrophic block — a-u-t-o-t-r-o-p-h-i-c block. So when the older literature uses vertical farm or urban greenhouse, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I wanna discuss is what urban futurists call the "integration pathway typology". When researchers map how cities embed autotrophic blocks into existing fabric, they sketch a graded typology running from retrofit basement installations through ground-floor commercial conversions to purpose-built podium structures. So, you know, you'll see blocks tucked under disused car parks — that's a retrofit basement. Or schemes that convert supermarket frontages — that's a ground-floor conversion. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the integration pathway typology. [pause:3s] Now, the forecast panel data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the five hundred municipal scenarios we surveyed across eight metropolitan regions last year, MOST predicted autotrophic-block coverage above the urban-food security threshold by 2040 — roughly sixty-four per cent. Only a few — about twelve per cent — forecast stagnation, and some — twenty-four per cent — projected uneven, district-by-district uptake. So expansion dominates numerically, but the stagnation tail, though modest, is theoretically significant for policy hedging. [pause:3s] A second key construct I wanna flag is "horizon dampening". This refers to a temporal pattern in which optimistic near-term forecasts compress toward the median as forecast year approaches — sometimes halving expected yield gains within five years. At Riverside metro, our team logged eighty-eight documented dampening episodes across the cohort during one fiscal year. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that technology adoption linearly accelerates urban-food self-sufficiency is, frankly, not supported. Most of the scenarios in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic acceleration as digital-twin maturity increased. Quite the opposite — many showed an S-shaped curve, with a plateau spike around the seventy-per-cent adoption mark, because regulatory ceilings stall further uptake. So the older "linear-tech-adoption" hypothesis, which predicts smooth acceleration, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Okay, let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT cross-domain integrated-panel state is what we're, gonna, kinda scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar — sorta the centrepiece. I want you to focus on the scenario-coding protocols specifically, not the digital-twin futures or the legacy Delphi instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: smart-city futures are a convergence-horizon problem, not a checklist; the technical term for closed-loop building-integrated food production is autotrophic block; expansion dominates forecasts at roughly sixty-four per cent; and the linear-tech-adoption hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine governance feedback loops. Thanks, you guys. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: Investing in strategic foresight allows governments to allocate resources pre-emptively rather than scrambling to react once a crisis has already materialised.
Robust scenario-modelling lets policymakers stress-test a decision against several plausible futures at once, rather than betting everything on a single, speculative guess.
Anticipating demographic shifts well in advance can spare a nation the worst of the fiscal shock that an ageing population would otherwise inflict on pension systems.
Long-range planning built around credible projections tends to stand the test of time far better than policies drafted purely in response to short-term political pressure.
Forecasts about the distant future remain inherently speculative, so resources channelled into elaborate contingency planning can ultimately prove to have been squandered.
An overreliance on a single favoured scenario can leave institutions dangerously unprepared the moment reality departs from the assumed trajectory.
Excessive futurology risks diverting funding from pressing present-day needs towards distant possibilities that may never actually come to pass.
A dystopian obsession with worst-case outcomes can breed public fatalism, discouraging the very innovation that might otherwise avert the feared crisis.
The accelerating pace of disruptive technologies, especially artificial intelligence, has made confident long-term forecasting far harder than it was a generation ago.
Shifting demography, most notably declining birth rates alongside rising longevity, is forcing economists to revisit assumptions that once seemed settled.
Growing awareness that an unprecedented climate or public-health emergency could strike with little warning has driven institutions to formalise foresight as a discipline in its own right.
Competitive pressure in business and geopolitics has made strategic foresight a survival necessity, since rivals who anticipate change first tend to seize a decisive advantage.
Where institutions genuinely embed foresight into decision-making, infrastructure and health systems tend to cope far better when an unprecedented shock eventually strikes.
Failure to heed early projections about population ageing has already left several pension systems facing a trajectory towards insolvency.
Widespread scepticism towards forecasting can lead societies to bury their heads in the sand, deferring painful but necessary reforms until crisis makes them unavoidable.
Chronic underinvestment in preparedness has, in some sectors, made a severe supply-chain disruption feel almost imminent rather than merely possible.
Distinguishing a plausible early warning from mere alarmism remains a persistent challenge, since both can sound equally urgent to policymakers.
Rare, high-impact events — often described as black swan occurrences — are, by definition, resistant to the kind of pattern-based forecasting most institutions rely on.
Balancing the moral urgency of present suffering against the abstract, speculative nature of long-term risk continues to divide budget committees the world over.
Communicating unprecedented but low-probability threats to a public that instinctively discounts distant dangers is a contentious communication challenge in itself.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Building antifragility into critical systems, so that they actually strengthen under stress rather than merely surviving it, is increasingly seen as wiser than chasing a single perfect prediction.
Governments can commission independent scenario-planning units tasked with mapping several plausible trajectories rather than issuing one over-confident projection.
Diversifying expert panels to include historians, scientists and ethicists helps ensure that speculative forecasts are stress-tested from multiple angles before being acted upon.
Embedding regular horizon-scanning exercises within ministries can help societies catch a sign of things to come long before a disruptive event becomes imminent.
Many optimists insist that disruptive innovation will keep solving problems as they arise, so meticulous long-term planning is ultimately an anxious waste of energy.
Others firmly believe that certain outcomes, from population ageing to resource strain, are now so close to inevitable that ignoring them borders on negligence.
A widespread, almost folk view holds that only time will tell which predictions prove accurate, and that confident forecasting is therefore inherently self-important.
Sceptics frequently point out that history's boldest forecasters have often been proven wrong, which fuels public distrust of anyone claiming genuine foresight.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: National governments bear primary responsibility for translating credible projections into concrete policy rather than leaving citizens to face an imminent shock unprepared.
Scientists and demographers have a duty to communicate plausible scenarios clearly, resisting the temptation to either sensationalise or downplay uncertain findings.
Corporations that profit from disruptive technologies arguably owe society a degree of strategic foresight about the social consequences their innovations may unleash.
Ordinary citizens also share some responsibility, since a populace that refuses to bury its head in the sand puts healthy pressure on leaders to plan responsibly.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although critics dismiss futurology as purely speculative, even an imperfect projection can guide policy far more reliably than proceeding with no forecast at all.
While some argue that a dystopian narrative around technology is needlessly alarmist, such warnings have occasionally proven prescient once the feared paradigm shift actually arrived.
It could be argued that resources spent on distant risk are wasted, yet ignoring a slow-moving but unprecedented threat such as climate change is arguably a graver error.
Sceptics claim forecasting inevitably fails, but proponents counter that the goal of good foresight is resilience across multiple scenarios, not a single infallible prophecy.
Forecasting itself is likely to shift away from single confident projections towards probabilistic ranges that openly acknowledge how speculative any distant estimate remains.
Artificial intelligence and vast datasets are expected to sharpen scenario-modelling, allowing forecasters to simulate far more plausible trajectories than manual analysis ever could.
Growing respect for rare, high-impact black swan events is set to push futurists towards designing antifragile systems rather than chasing ever more precise point predictions.
As institutions learn from past forecasting failures, humility is likely to become the norm, with experts more openly conceding that only time will tell which scenario ultimately unfolds.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas earlier generations of forecasters leaned almost entirely on historical trend lines, today's analysts increasingly combine demography, climate data and computational scenario-modelling.
Compared with visionaries who were once dismissed as ahead of their time, contemporary futurists benefit from far richer data yet still cannot escape genuine uncertainty.
Unlike the confident, singular forecasts once favoured by planners, modern foresight practice openly weighs several competing trajectories side by side.
In contrast to societies that historically chose to bury their heads in the sand, many nations now treat strategic foresight as a core function of government rather than an afterthought.
Long-range demographic projections showing a growing share of elderly citizens can be cited as evidence that pension reform is no longer optional.

A historical case in which an inventor or thinker was ridiculed for being ahead of their time, only for their idea to later stand the test of time, illustrates how easily society dismisses genuine foresight.
The abrupt, largely unforeseen arrival of a global pandemic serves as a textbook black swan example of how quickly a plausible but unlikely scenario can become reality.
Corporate case studies of firms that failed to anticipate a disruptive technology, only to see the writing on the wall too late, are often cited as cautionary evidence in business forecasting.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Whether societies should anchor themselves in present-day concerns or invest heavily in long-term forecasting has become an increasingly contested question. While both positions have intuitive appeal, I lean towards the view that rigorous long-term planning is indispensable, even if it must be tempered by present realities.

Those who favour focusing on the present argue, not unreasonably, that the future is inherently unpredictable. Rapid technological disruptions — most notably the rise of generative AI — have rendered many predictions from a decade ago almost laughable, which suggests that over-speculating may waste scarce public resources. Furthermore, in regions where immediate poverty and food insecurity persist, channelling funds into distant scenarios can seem morally questionable when so many citizens require help today. It is the urgency of present suffering, in short, that gives this position its force.

On the other hand, advocates of long-term planning point out that some threats are too consequential to ignore. Climate tipping points, demographic shifts and pandemics are likely to produce cataclysmic outcomes if left unaddressed, and burying our heads in the sand virtually guarantees an inadequate response. The silver tsunami of ageing populations, for instance, was foreseen by demographers decades ago, yet many governments still appear unprepared. Without anticipation, infrastructure, pensions and healthcare systems are bound to buckle under pressure.

In my view, the two perspectives are less opposed than they first appear. While immediate problems clearly demand attention, ignoring the long term is a form of negligence that future generations will pay for. A balanced approach — addressing present needs while quietly preparing for foreseeable challenges — strikes me as the most responsible path forward, since even an imperfect projection is preferable to none at all.

Few questions divide policymakers and philosophers as sharply as whether to privilege immediate concerns or commit to rigorous long-term planning. Although both stances carry weight, I would argue, with some caution, that long-range anticipation is no longer optional in an age of cascading risks, even if it must be balanced against present needs.

The case for present-focused governance is not without merit. The future, after all, is inherently opaque; the exponential pace of technological disruption — particularly in artificial intelligence and biotechnology — has rendered many earlier projections obsolete. So volatile is contemporary scenario-modelling that futurists themselves now speak in terms of plausibility ranges rather than firm forecasts. Moreover, in low-income societies, the moral imperative to alleviate immediate poverty arguably trumps speculative investment in distant possibilities; the elderly going hungry today cannot be sustained by tomorrow's smart cities.

Yet the counter-argument is equally formidable. Were governments to abandon long-term planning, the demographic time bomb — the projected doubling of the global over-sixty population by 2050 — would render pension and healthcare systems insolvent. Equally, climate science has identified tipping points beyond which damage becomes irreversible; failing to act on such projections amounts, in effect, to wilful negligence. The anticipation of unprecedented shocks, from pandemics to mass displacement, is bound to become a defining feature of competent statecraft.

In my considered opinion, the dichotomy is somewhat misleading. The genuine task is not to choose between present and future but to allocate cognitive and fiscal bandwidth across both. It is the integration of immediate welfare with rigorous scenario-modelling that will most likely produce resilient societies. To dismiss long-term planning as speculative luxury is, in my view, to repeat the very mistakes that left so many nations exposed during the recent pandemic — a failure of foresight that future generations are unlikely to forgive.

solutions.text: PHẦN A — Viết lại câu (12 items)
Viết lại mỗi câu dưới đây dùng TỪ GỢI Ý (in hoa), giữ nguyên nghĩa và đúng dạng/collocation.
1. Many analysts believe that some form of economic disruption is (INEVITABLE) as automation spreads across traditional industries.
2. City planners warn that a housing shortage looks (IMMINENT) unless new construction is authorised within the next few years.
3. Changing (DEMOGRAPHY), particularly an ageing population, is likely to place growing strain on healthcare and pension systems.
4. Government (PROJECTIONS) suggest that renewable energy could supply most of the national grid within a few decades.
5. Urban planners often model a worst-case (SCENARIO) to make sure new infrastructure can cope with future population growth.
6. The pace of change in artificial intelligence over the past few years has been genuinely (UNPRECEDENTED).
7. It would be unwise to (SPECULATE) too confidently about exactly which jobs will disappear, since technology evolves unpredictably.
8. Many economists argue that (DISRUPTIVE) technologies such as automation and AI will fundamentally reorganise the labour market.
9. Strategic (FORESIGHT) allows governments to prepare for demographic and environmental pressures long before a crisis erupts.
10. Some novelists imagine a (DYSTOPIAN) future in which surveillance technology has eroded nearly all personal privacy.
11. The shift towards remote working during recent years represents a genuine (PARADIGM SHIFT) in how organisations think about productivity.
12. If current trends continue, the (TRAJECTORY) of global urbanisation points towards ever larger and more crowded megacities.
PHẦN B — Nâng cấp câu — Ladder (Band 6 → 7 → 8) (8 items)
Nâng cấp câu Band 6 cho sẵn lên Band 7 rồi Band 8 (giữ nguyên ý, nâng từ vựng + cấu trúc).

PHẦN A: 1. Many analysts believe that some form of economic disruption is inevitable as automation spreads across traditional industries. — "Inevitable" nghĩa là "không thể tránh khỏi"; thường đi với "seem/become inevitable", khác với "unpredictable" (không thể đoán trước). 2. City planners warn that a housing shortage looks imminent unless new construction is authorised within the next few years. — "Imminent" chỉ điều "sắp xảy ra, cận kề"; hay đi với "imminent danger/collapse/breakthrough". 3. Changing demography, particularly an ageing population, is likely to place growing strain on healthcare and pension systems. — "Demography" là ngành nghiên cứu dân số; phân biệt với "demographics" (số liệu dân số cụ thể). 4. Government projections suggest that renewable energy could supply most of the national grid within a few decades. — "Projections" (số nhiều) chỉ các dự báo dựa trên xu hướng hiện tại, thường đi với "economic/population projections". 5. Urban planners often model a worst-case scenario to make sure new infrastructure can cope with future population growth. — "Scenario" là kịch bản/tình huống giả định; collocation phổ biến "a worst-case scenario", "a plausible scenario". 6. The pace of change in artificial intelligence over the past few years has been genuinely unprecedented. — "Unprecedented" nghĩa là "chưa từng có tiền lệ"; hay đi với "unprecedented levels/scale/growth". 7. It would be unwise to speculate too confidently about exactly which jobs will disappear, since technology evolves unpredictably. — "Speculate" là suy đoán không có bằng chứng chắc chắn; giới từ đi kèm là "about/on", không dùng "for". 8. Many economists argue that disruptive technologies such as automation and AI will fundamentally reorganise the labour market. — "Disruptive" trong ngữ cảnh công nghệ/kinh doanh mang nghĩa tích cực (đột phá), không phải nghĩa tiêu cực thông thường. 9. Strategic foresight allows governments to prepare for demographic and environmental pressures long before a crisis erupts. — "Foresight" là danh từ không đếm được, chỉ khả năng nhìn xa trông rộng; trái nghĩa với "hindsight". 10. Some novelists imagine a dystopian future in which surveillance technology has eroded nearly all personal privacy. — "Dystopian" mô tả một xã hội tương lai đen tối, áp bức; trái nghĩa với "utopian". 11. The shift towards remote working during recent years represents a genuine paradigm shift in how organisations think about productivity. — "Paradigm shift" là sự thay đổi căn bản trong tư duy/cách tiếp cận; chữ "g" trong "paradigm" câm khi phát âm. 12. If current trends continue, the trajectory of global urbanisation points towards ever larger and more crowded megacities. — "Trajectory" chỉ hướng phát triển của một xu hướng; ở đây dùng nghĩa ẩn dụ, không phải nghĩa vật lý.

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: It is likely that remote working will become increasingly common in the years ahead. Band 8: Remote working looks set to become the norm rather than the exception, as organisations increasingly embrace flexible arrangements. 2. Band 7: Many experts predict that automation will eliminate certain types of jobs. Band 8: Many experts argue that disruptive automation will render a range of routine occupations largely obsolete, even if entirely new roles emerge in their place. 3. Band 7: Nobody can predict with certainty what society will look like in fifty years' time. Band 8: Given how inherently speculative long-range forecasting is, it seems unwise to claim any certainty about society half a century from now. 4. Band 7: Governments should show foresight and plan for problems before a crisis develops. Band 8: Were governments to cultivate greater strategic foresight, many looming crises might be pre-empted rather than merely managed after the fact. 5. Band 7: New inventions often bring about unexpected changes in the way people live. Band 8: It is often disruptive innovation, rather than incremental progress, that triggers a genuine paradigm shift in everyday life. 6. Band 7: Some predictions turn out to be inaccurate because circumstances change so rapidly. Band 8: Not only do circumstances shift unpredictably, but forecasts that once seemed plausible may well prove wide of the mark within a matter of years. 7. Band 7: It is probable that cities will expand considerably over the coming decades. Band 8: Should current demographic trends persist, our cities' trajectory points towards unprecedented levels of urban density within a generation. 8. Band 7: It is difficult to know for certain whether a new technology will transform society. Band 8: Whether a given technology will prove genuinely transformative or merely a passing trend is something only time will tell.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Silver Tsunami: The global population of people aged 60 and over is expected to double to 2.1 billion by 2050, placing an unprecedented strain on national pension schemes and healthcare infrastructure.
Urbanization Projections: The UN projects that by 2050, 68% of the world population will live in urban areas, requiring a massive paradigm shift in sustainable city planning (smart cities).
Climate Tipping Points: Scientists warn that surpassing 1.5°C of global warming could trigger irreversible cataclysmic events, such as the complete melting of the Greenland ice sheet.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: The Aging Population (Is Longevity a blessing or a curse?)

A Blessing (Optimistic): Older individuals possess immense wisdom and experience, providing free childcare (grandparents) and continuing to contribute to the "silver economy"; it reflects humanity's ultimate triumph over disease.

A Curse (Pessimistic): An aging demographic inevitably shrinks the active workforce, severely reducing tax revenues while simultaneously skyrocketing public expenditure on chronic healthcare and pensions.
Topic: Overpopulation & Resource Scarcity
The Threat: Continuous population growth on a planet with finite resources is a recipe for a dystopian future; it accelerates deforestation, water scarcity, and greenhouse gas emissions.
The Solution: Education and female empowerment in developing nations consistently lead to lower birth rates; transitioning to lab-grown meats and vertical farming can sustainably feed billions.
Topic: Predicting the Future (Should we plan ahead or live in the present?)
Why we must plan: Unforeseen cataclysmic events (pandemics, natural disasters) require rigorous anticipation and robust infrastructure; "burying our heads in the sand" ensures our downfall.

Why we shouldn't over-speculate: The future is inherently unpredictable due to rapid technological disruptions (like AI); over-planning wastes current resources that could be used to alleviate immediate poverty today.
(Cấu trúc diễn đạt Khả năng & Tính chắc chắn - Điểm ngữ pháp "ăn điểm" (Band 7.5+) giúp bạn thay thế các từ đơn điệu như "will", "maybe", hay "perhaps" khi đưa ra Dự đoán trong IELTS Writing Task 2).

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~272 words)

The prediction I'd like to talk about is one I genuinely believe will reshape the 21st century: that climate-induced mass migration will become the defining geopolitical challenge of the next thirty years. This forecast has been articulated most prominently by the World Bank in its 2021 Groundswell Report, which projected that up to 216 million people could become internal climate migrants by 2050.

The prediction is built on extensively peer-reviewed climate models. As global temperatures continue rising — currently tracking towards 2.7°C of warming this century according to the latest UNEP Emissions Gap Report — entire regions will likely become functionally uninhabitable due to extreme heat, sea-level rise, desertification, and water scarcity.

What makes this particularly chilling is the timeline: this isn't a distant dystopian scenario but something already unfolding. The Mekong Delta in my own country is projected to lose roughly 40% of its arable land by 2050, potentially displacing 12 million Vietnamese. Bangladesh faces even starker numbers, with up to 18 million people anticipated to migrate by mid-century.

Several factors convince me this prediction is unfortunately bound to materialise. Firstly, the climate physics is essentially locked in — even immediate net-zero would not reverse the warming already underway. Secondly, despite COP commitments, global emissions hit a record high in 2023, suggesting we're nowhere near the trajectory needed for the IPCC's 1.5°C pathway. And thirdly, what really seals it for me is that historical precedents — from the Syrian drought-driven displacement to Pacific Island evacuations — show that political systems consistently underestimate climate migration until it becomes a crisis.
Granted, I'd love to be proven wrong, but the writing, as they say, is on the wall.

blocks.text: Q1: Can we trust expert predictions?

Point: Expert predictions deserve qualified rather than blind trust — they're considerably more reliable than intuition or speculation, but they also carry systematic biases that the public often overlooks.

Explain: The fundamental issue is that experts excel within their domain of training but tend to be overconfident in cross-disciplinary contexts, and they're particularly poor at predicting tail events — the rare, high-impact occurrences that actually matter most. Philip Tetlock's landmark 20-year study of expert political forecasts found that specialists performed only marginally better than random chance on long-horizon predictions.

Example: The 2008 financial crisis offers a stark illustration: virtually no mainstream economists predicted it, despite warning signs being visible to outliers like Nouriel Roubini. Conversely, climate scientists have a remarkable track record — the temperature projections made by Hansen et al. in 1988 have proven accurate to within 0.1°C over three decades. The difference, arguably, lies in domains with well-understood physics versus those involving human behaviour.

Link: So rather than trusting experts uncritically or dismissing them as elites, the most rational approach is to consult diverse expert panels — what's called "superforecasting" — and weight predictions according to the underlying methodology's track record.
Q2: Will AI cause mass unemployment?
Point: While AI will undoubtedly disrupt enormous swathes of the labour market, I'd argue the "mass unemployment" framing somewhat misrepresents what's likely to unfold over the next two decades.

Explain: The reason previous technological revolutions — from mechanisation to computerisation — didn't produce permanent mass unemployment is that automation typically eliminates specific tasks rather than entire occupations, and the productivity gains generated tend to create new categories of work that didn't previously exist. That said, AI is qualitatively different because it targets cognitive rather than physical labour, which may compress adjustment timelines considerably.

Example: A widely-cited 2023 Goldman Sachs report estimated that 300 million full-time jobs globally are exposed to some degree of AI automation, with legal services, administrative work, and entry-level coding being particularly vulnerable. However, the IMF's parallel analysis found that roughly 40% of those exposed jobs would be augmented rather than replaced. The Industrial Revolution provides instructive precedent: weavers were displaced, but the textile workforce eventually grew tenfold over the following century.

Link: So the more likely scenario isn't mass unemployment but rather a turbulent decade of occupational restructuring — and the policy challenge is less about preventing AI than about ensuring the transition doesn't leave entire generations behind.
Q3: Should we plan for centuries ahead?

Point: I'd argue that long-horizon planning — spanning centuries rather than electoral cycles — is not merely desirable but increasingly imperative, though it must be balanced against pressing immediate needs.

Explain: The philosophical case for longtermism, articulated by thinkers like Derek Parfit and more recently William MacAskill, rests on the observation that future generations vastly outnumber the present one, yet have no political voice. Decisions made today on climate, biodiversity, and nuclear waste will reverberate for thousands of years, which generates a moral obligation we routinely ignore.

Example: Finland's nuclear waste repository Onkalo provides a fascinating real-world example: designed to safely contain spent fuel for 100,000 years, it required engineering for tectonic shifts, ice ages, and linguistic drift — warning signs had to communicate across civilisational collapse. By contrast, most democracies struggle to plan beyond five-year cycles, which is precisely why infrastructure deficits compound. The Japanese concept of "shichidai" — planning seven generations ahead — has begun influencing Western policy discussions.

Link: Ultimately, while we cannot reasonably predict centuries with precision, we can identify decisions with long-lasting consequences and apply appropriate caution — what's needed isn't a crystal ball but rather institutional humility about irreversibility.
T24 — THE FUTURE & PREDICTIONS
Lecture title: "Scenario Planning, Black Swans and the Mirage of Technological Singularity"
1. Section Type

IELTS Listening — Section 4 (academic lecture in futures studies and risk theory, ~3:00 minutes). Speaker: Professor Reuben Saltzman, Department of Strategic Foresight. Multiple-choice + note-completion hybrid.
2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

rows: a strategic method that maps multiple plausible futures
a rare, high-impact event that is rationalised only in hindsight
a hypothesised point when machine intelligence overtakes human
the disciplined anticipation of long-range change
reasonable and credible, though not necessarily certain

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas
The lecturer will probably defend scenario planning against the demand for single-point forecasts.
Black swan events may be reframed not as unpredictable but as underanticipated.
The technological singularity will likely be debunked as speculative rather than imminent.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about how organisations should think about the future without pretending they can predict it. I want to address three frameworks: scenario planning, black swan theory, and the much-hyped technological singularity. The intellectual hygiene around each is, frankly, patchy.

> Let me begin with scenario planning, pioneered at Royal Dutch Shell in the 1970s under Pierre Wack. The discipline does not generate a single forecast. Instead, it constructs three or four internally coherent, mutually exclusive futures — say, a high-oil-price world, a low-carbon world, a fragmented-geopolitics world — and stress-tests an organisation's strategy against each. The genius of the method, captured in Shell's anticipation of the 1973 oil shock, lies precisely in its refusal to bet on one path. A robust strategy, in this view, is one that does not catastrophically fail in any plausible scenario.

> Now, black swans. The Lebanese-American thinker Nassim Nicholas Taleb popularised the concept in 2007. A black swan is an event with three properties: it is rare, it has outsized impact, and it is rationalised, with embarrassing ease, after the fact. The 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic are textbook cases. Taleb's deeper warning is that we systematically underestimate the fat tail of low-probability, high-consequence events because human cognition is anchored to bell-curve intuitions. The remedy is not better forecasting; it is antifragility — building systems that gain from disorder rather than merely survive it.

Let me push back on something I may have implied — that these three frameworks sit in tidy isolation. They don't; in practice they interfere with one another, sometimes destructively. Here's the tension. Scenario planning, done well, is supposed to expand the range of futures you take seriously. But there's a documented failure mode — call it the plausibility trap. Because scenarios have to be coherent and narratable to be useful to a board, planners tend to exclude the genuinely weird, the un-narratable, the events that defy a clean storyline. [pause] And those, of course, are precisely the black swans. So the very discipline that's meant to inoculate you against surprise can, um, quietly anaesthetise you to the surprises that matter most.

Now let me complicate Taleb a little, in fairness to his critics. There's a sharp objection that the black-swan label is, retrospectively, too elastic — that almost any large shock gets reclassified as unforeseeable after the fact, which conveniently absolves the people who should have foreseen it. Take 2008. Several economists — Roubini, Rajan — did warn of systemic fragility in the housing-credit chain. So was the crisis a true black swan, or what Michele Wucker later called a grey rhino: a high-probability, high-impact threat charging straight at us that we collectively chose to ignore? [pause] That distinction isn't pedantic. It changes the policy prescription entirely — from "build antifragile buffers against the unknowable" to "stop rewarding institutions for averting their eyes from the known."

And on the singularity, one nuance worth banking. Even if Kurzweil's recursive-self-improvement timeline is fantasy, the rhetorical function of the prediction is real: it shapes where venture capital flows and which risks regulators feel licensed to defer. Well, a forecast doesn't need to be accurate to be consequential. Which is the uncomfortable thread tying all three together — the way our images of the future govern present action — and that brings us squarely to the institutional response I want to sketch next…

> Finally, the technological singularity. Proponents like Ray Kurzweil project a moment around 2045 when artificial intelligence will recursively self-improve. The claim is bold but, on inspection, deeply speculative. There is no rigorous physical theory predicting it. Treat it, please, as conjecture, not prophecy. Now, looking at handout four…

Q2 cue: the discourse marker "The genius of the method… lies precisely in…" — flags a thesis statement.
Q3 cue: the date-after-attribution "Nassim Nicholas Taleb popularised the concept in 2007" — year follows the verb.
Q4 cue: the contrastive "The remedy is not better forecasting; it is antifragility" — negation-then-affirmation structure.
Q5 cue: the closing imperative "Treat it, please, as __________, not prophecy" — answer is contrasted with "prophecy".

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~194 từ)

The bar chart provides the projected annual growth rates of six economic sectors in 2030, while the pie chart shows each sector's share of total GDP in 2024, the two being measured in different units.
Overall, a striking inverse pattern emerges: the sectors that currently dominate GDP are forecast to grow most slowly, whereas the smaller, emerging sectors are poised to expand most rapidly.

Turning first to the bar chart, AI & Software is projected to grow by 14.2% in 2030, the highest figure shown, followed by Renewable Energy at 11.6% and Biotech at 9.8%. By contrast, the established sectors post sluggish gains, with Manufacturing rising by just 3.1% and Retail by only 2.4%, while Fossil Fuels alone is set to contract, declining by 1.7%.

The pie chart, however, paints an almost opposite picture for 2024. Manufacturing commands the largest slice at 28%, trailed by Retail at 22% and Fossil Fuels at 18%; together these three incumbents account for more than two-thirds of GDP. Meanwhile, AI & Software (13%), Renewable Energy (11%) and Biotech (8%) hold only around a third between them, implying that their rapid expansion could substantially reshape the economy by 2030.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~197 từ)

The bar chart sets out the projected annual growth rates of six economic sectors in 2030, whereas the pie chart records each sector's share of total GDP in 2024, the two thus capturing momentum and scale respectively.

What stands out most clearly is the inverse relationship binding the panels together: the sectors that command the largest share of output today are precisely those projected to grow most feebly, while the smallest incumbents appear poised for the steepest expansion.

Considering the bar chart first, AI & Software is forecast to surge by 14.2% in 2030, comfortably the highest figure, with Renewable Energy and Biotech at 11.6% and 9.8%. So muted is the outlook for the traditional sectors that Manufacturing manages only 3.1% and Retail a mere 2.4%, while Fossil Fuels alone contracts, slipping by 1.7%.

The pie chart, by contrast, inverts this hierarchy entirely. Manufacturing accounts for the dominant 28% of GDP, ahead of Retail at 22% and Fossil Fuels at 18%, so that the three slow-growing incumbents together absorb fully 68% of output. The three high-growth fields share just 32% between them — a disparity implying that their dynamism could decisively recast the economy within the decade.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 nâng câu Overview lên tầng nhận định sắc hơn — gọi tên thẳng 'inverse relationship binding the panels together' và 'primed for substantial reordering' — thay vì chỉ mô tả 'inverse pattern emerges' như Band 7, thể hiện Task Achievement cao hơn.

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày hơn: đảo ngữ ('So muted is the outlook for the traditional sectors that ...'), câu chẻ nhấn mạnh ('are precisely those projected to grow most feebly') và động từ giàu sắc thái ('surge', 'slipping', 'recast'), trong khi Band 7 dựa nhiều vào 'followed by / By contrast'.

•  Band 8 xử lý so sánh hai biểu đồ chặt hơn: cộng dồn '68%' incumbents vs '32%' high-growth để định lượng độ chênh, còn Band 7 chỉ nói 'more than two-thirds' và 'around a third' — Band 8 do đó chính xác và mạch lạc hơn ở khâu Coherence.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Nhận diện đây là combo bar+pie ĐO BẰNG HAI ĐƠN VỊ khác nhau (growth % vs GDP share %): ngay câu mở phải nói rõ điều này để tránh trộn lẫn số liệu giữa hai bảng.
•  Tìm 'mỏ neo' cho Overview là MỐI QUAN HỆ NGHỊCH giữa hai biểu đồ (ngành lớn hiện tại ↔ tăng trưởng yếu; ngành nhỏ ↔ tăng trưởng mạnh) — đây là đặc điểm nổi bật nhất, viết không kèm số liệu.

•  Chia thân bài theo từng biểu đồ: một đoạn cho bar (cao→thấp: AI 14.2 > Renewables 11.6 > Biotech 9.8 > Manufacturing 3.1 > Retail 2.4 > Fossil Fuels –1.7), một đoạn cho pie (Manufacturing 28 > Retail 22 > Fossil 18 > AI 13 > Renewables 11 > Biotech 8).
•  Trong đoạn pie, chèn câu so sánh chéo với bar để làm bật quan hệ nghịch (ví dụ Manufacturing chiếm 28% GDP nhưng chỉ tăng 3.1%) — đây là điểm 'make comparisons where relevant' giám khảo tìm.
•  Dùng động từ tăng/giảm đa dạng và chính xác: surge/expand cho tăng mạnh, post sluggish gains/crawl cho tăng yếu, contract/slip cho giảm — và luôn gắn số liệu đúng với từng panel.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~280 words)

Whether societies should anchor themselves in present-day concerns or invest heavily in long-term forecasting has become an increasingly contested question. While both positions have intuitive appeal, I lean towards the view that rigorous long-term planning is indispensable, even if it must be tempered by present realities.

Those who favour focusing on the present argue, not unreasonably, that the future is inherently unpredictable. Rapid technological disruptions — most notably the rise of generative AI — have rendered many predictions from a decade ago almost laughable, which suggests that over-speculating may waste scarce public resources. Furthermore, in regions where immediate poverty and food insecurity persist, channelling funds into distant scenarios can seem morally questionable when so many citizens require help today. It is the urgency of present suffering, in short, that gives this position its force.

On the other hand, advocates of long-term planning point out that some threats are too consequential to ignore. Climate tipping points, demographic shifts and pandemics are likely to produce cataclysmic outcomes if left unaddressed, and burying our heads in the sand virtually guarantees an inadequate response. The silver tsunami of ageing populations, for instance, was foreseen by demographers decades ago, yet many governments still appear unprepared. Without anticipation, infrastructure, pensions and healthcare systems are bound to buckle under pressure.

In my view, the two perspectives are less opposed than they first appear. While immediate problems clearly demand attention, ignoring the long term is a form of negligence that future generations will pay for. A balanced approach — addressing present needs while quietly preparing for foreseeable challenges — strikes me as the most responsible path forward, since even an imperfect projection is preferable to none at all.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~301 words)

Few questions divide policymakers and philosophers as sharply as whether to privilege immediate concerns or commit to rigorous long-term planning. Although both stances carry weight, I would argue, with some caution, that long-range anticipation is no longer optional in an age of cascading risks, even if it must be balanced against present needs.

The case for present-focused governance is not without merit. The future, after all, is inherently opaque; the exponential pace of technological disruption — particularly in artificial intelligence and biotechnology — has rendered many earlier projections obsolete. So volatile is contemporary scenario-modelling that futurists themselves now speak in terms of plausibility ranges rather than firm forecasts. Moreover, in low-income societies, the moral imperative to alleviate immediate poverty arguably trumps speculative investment in distant possibilities; the elderly going hungry today cannot be sustained by tomorrow's smart cities.

Yet the counter-argument is equally formidable. Were governments to abandon long-term planning, the demographic time bomb — the projected doubling of the global over-sixty population by 2050 — would render pension and healthcare systems insolvent. Equally, climate science has identified tipping points beyond which damage becomes irreversible; failing to act on such projections amounts, in effect, to wilful negligence. The anticipation of unprecedented shocks, from pandemics to mass displacement, is bound to become a defining feature of competent statecraft.

In my considered opinion, the dichotomy is somewhat misleading. The genuine task is not to choose between present and future but to allocate cognitive and fiscal bandwidth across both. It is the integration of immediate welfare with rigorous scenario-modelling that will most likely produce resilient societies. To dismiss long-term planning as speculative luxury is, in my view, to repeat the very mistakes that left so many nations exposed during the recent pandemic — a failure of foresight that future generations are unlikely to forgive.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 mở bài và thesis ở register cao hơn ('cascading risks', 'long-range anticipation is no longer optional') và bổ sung nhượng bộ tinh tế ('even if it must be balanced against present needs'), thể hiện lập trường sắc nét hơn so với Band 7.

•  Band 8 dùng dày các cấu trúc bậc cao: đảo ngữ ('So volatile is contemporary scenario-modelling that ...'), điều kiện đảo ('Were governments to abandon long-term planning ...'), câu chẻ ('It is the integration ... that ...') và danh hoá ('the exponential pace of technological disruption', 'the anticipation of unprecedented shocks'), trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft và nhiều cụm hơi đời thường ('almost laughable', 'burying our heads in the sand').

•  Band 8 lập luận chặt hơn ở phần phản biện — định lượng rủi ro ('projected doubling of the over-sixty population by 2050') và phân biệt rõ 'plausibility ranges' với 'firm forecasts' — đồng thời cohesion mượt hơn ('Yet ... Equally ... In my considered opinion'), nâng Coherence & Task Response một bậc.
